Unlike English, where gender is usually biological (he/she/it), Sanskrit gender is grammatical and lexical.

There are three main reasons why a word like Madhu, Cañcu, or Vāri might appear in different genders.

docs.title: 1. The Word is an Adjective (Viśeṣaṇa)
docs.text:
This is the most common reason. In Sanskrit, adjectives do not have a gender of their own; they take the gender of the noun they describe.

If a word like Madhu (which usually means honey) is used to mean "sweet" or "pleasant," it becomes an adjective. Therefore, it changes to match the noun.

  • Masculine: Madhuḥ (Sweet/Pleasant)
    • Example: मधुः अनिलः (Madhuḥ anilaḥ) — A pleasant breeze.
  • Feminine: Madhvī or Madhuḥ (Sweet)
    • Example: मध्वी लता (Madhvī latā) — A sweet/lovely creeper (vine).
  • Neuter: Madhu (Sweet)
    • Example: मधु फलम् (Madhu phalam) — A sweet fruit.

docs.title: 2. Semantic Variation (Same Word, Different Meanings)
docs.text:
Sometimes, a word has the exact same spelling/pronunciation, but the gender changes the meaning entirely.

Example: Madhu * Neuter (Madhu): Honey, nectar. * Usage: इदं मधु अस्ति (Idam madhu asti) — This is honey. * Masculine (Madhuḥ): Name of a demon (killed by Vishnu), the season of Spring (Vasanta), or the Asoka tree. * Usage: मधुः आगच्छति (Madhuḥ āgacchati) — Spring is coming.

Example: Cañcu * Feminine (Cañcūḥ or Cañcuḥ): A beak (of a bird). * Usage: पक्षिणः चञ्चूः तीक्ष्णा (Pakṣiṇaḥ cañcūḥ tīkṣṇā) — The bird's beak is sharp. * Masculine (Cañcuḥ): Used in compounds to mean "famous for" or "clever in." * Usage: विद्याचञ्चुः (Vidyā-cañcuḥ) — One who is famous for his knowledge.

Example: Mitra * Neuter (Mitram): A friend. * Usage: मम मित्रम् (Mama mitram) — My friend. * Masculine (Mitraḥ): The Sun (Vedic deity). * Usage: मित्राय नमः (Mitrāya namaḥ) — Salutations to the Sun.

docs.title: 3. Grammatical Compounds (Bahuvrīhi Samāsa)
docs.text:
This is a slightly advanced but very common reason. Even if a word is inherently Neuter (like Vāri - water), it can take Masculine or Feminine endings if it is part of a compound word describing a person or object.

Example: Vāri (Water - usually Neuter) If we describe a pot that contains water, we might say "That which has water." * Neuter: वारि (Vāri) — Water. * Masculine usage in compound: पीतवारिः (Pīta-vāriḥ) — "He who has drunk water." * Here, because the compound describes a "He" (Masculine), the word Vāri takes a masculine declension (Visarga) at the end, even though water itself is neuter.

docs.title: 1. Madhu (मधु)
docs.text:
• Neuter: Honey, nectar, milk.
  • Masculine: The month of Chaitra, Spring, Name of a Demon.
  • Adjective (All 3 genders): Sweet, delicious, pleasant.

docs.title: 2. Cañcu (चञ्चु)
docs.text:
• Feminine: A bird's beak.
  • Masculine: A name of a caste/tribe; also used as an adjective for "skilled" or "famous."
  • Neuter: (Rare) Sometimes used for a particular plant or castor oil.

docs.title: 3. Vāri (वारि)
docs.text:
• Neuter: Water. (This is 99% of the usage).
  • Feminine: A specific vessel for holding liquor (very rare dictionary definition).
  • Masculine/Feminine: Only when used as the last member of a compound adjective (e.g., sūta-vāriḥ - one who has poured out water).

docs.title: How to know which one to use?
docs.text:
1. Context is King: If you are talking about eating, Madhu is neuter (honey). If you are talking about the calendar, Madhu is masculine (Spring).
  2. Look at the Adjectives: If the word is qualifying something else (e.g., "The sweet voice"), it changes gender to match the voice.
  3. docs.title: 1. The Nimitta for 8.2.76 (vorupadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ)
docs.text:
The "missing" condition is supplied by the Adhikāra (governing header) of this section. This sūtra falls under the governing rule 8.1.16 "पदस्य" (padasya).

  • The Condition: The operation happens when the root (dhātu) ending in 'r' or 'v' is situated at the end of a Pada (Padānta).
  • Explanation: The sūtra means: The penultimate (upadhā) 'ik' letter of a root ending in 'r' or 'v' becomes long (dīrgha) when it is at the end of a Pada.
  • Example:
    • Take the root गिर् (gir).
    • In the nominative singular (prathamā ekavacana), the su suffix is elided (deleted). The remaining form is gir.
    • Because "gir" is now a Pada, rule 8.2.76 applies.
    • Result: गीर् (gīr) -> (becomes gīḥ via Visarga Sandhi).

So, the answer to your first question: The nimitta is Padānta (being at the end of a word). It does not require a specific following letter; rather, it requires the absence of a following letter that would prevent it from being a pada-final.

docs.title: 2. The Purpose of 8.2.77 (hali cha)
docs.text:
If 8.2.76 already causes lengthening, why do we need "हलि च" (hali cha)?

  • The Problem: 8.2.76 only works if the root is at the end of the word (padānta). But often, roots appear in the middle of a word, followed by suffixes starting with consonants. In those cases, the root is usually not a Pada (it is an aṅga).
  • The Solution: 8.2.77 says: "And also (cha) when followed by a Hal (consonant)."

  • The Purpose: This sūtra extends the lengthening rule to situations where the root is apadānta (not at the end of a word) but is followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant.

  • Example (as seen in your screenshot):

    • दीव्यति (dīvyati).
    • Root: दिव् (div) + Suffix य (ya) (śyan) + ti.
    • Here, div is NOT at the end of the word (padānta), so 8.2.76 cannot apply.
    • However, div is followed by 'y', which is a Hal (consonant).
    • Therefore, by 8.2.77 Hali cha, the 'i' becomes 'ī'.
    • Result: dīv-ya-ti.

docs.title: Summary of the Distinction
docs.text:
1. Sūtra 8.2.76: Applies at the end of a word (Padānta).
  2. Sūtra 8.2.77: Applies in the middle of a word (Apadānta), specifically when followed by a consonant (Hali).

docs.title: 1. Translation of the Mahabhasya Quote
docs.text:
Sanskrit Text:

"कथम् ? प्रत्यङ्गवर्ती लोको लक्ष्यते । तद्यथा—पुरुषोऽयं प्रातरुत्थाय यान्यस्य प्रति शरीरं कार्याणि तानि तावत्करोति, ततः सुहृदां ततः सम्बन्धिनाम् ।" (महाभाष्यम् १.१.५७)

Word-for-Word Analysis: * Katham?: How (is this justified)? * Pratyangavarti: Turning towards the inner limbs/body (focused on the internal/proximate). * Loko lakshyate: The world (common people/behavior) is observed [to be]. * Tadyatha: Just as / For example. * Purusho'yam: This person / A man. * Pratarutthaya: Having risen in the morning. * Yanyasya: Those which are his... * Prati shariram karyani: Tasks concerning the body (personal hygiene, etc.). * Tani tavat karoti: He does those first. * Tatah suhrdam: Then [the tasks] of friends. * Tatah sambandhinam: Then [the tasks] of relatives.

English Translation:

"How is this? The world is observed to prioritize what is internal (closest to the self). For example, a person, having risen in the morning, first performs those tasks which concern his own body (like bathing, brushing teeth). Only then does he attend to the tasks of his friends, and after that, the tasks of his relatives."

docs.title: 2. Meaning of the Paribhasha
docs.text:
"असिद्धं बहिरङ्गमन्तरङ्गे"

  • Asiddham: Not accomplished; considered invalid or as if it has not happened.
  • Bahirangam: External; an operation based on external or more numerous causes.
  • Antarange: (When) internal; when an operation based on internal or fewer causes (is to be applied).

Core Principle: When an Antaranga (internal) operation and a Bahiranga (external) operation are simultaneously applicable, or when they interact, the Bahiranga operation is considered "Asiddha" (non-existent) with respect to the Antaranga operation. Therefore, the Antaranga operation takes precedence and is applied first.

Definition of Internal (Antaranga) vs. External (Bahiranga): Grammarians define "Internal" based on the causes (Nimitta) of the operation: 1. Alpa-nimitta (Fewer causes): Antaranga. 2. Purva-upasthita-nimitta (Causes present earlier in the sequence): Antaranga. 3. Antah-karya (Internal processing): Operations within the dhātu (root) or between root and upasarga are internal compared to those involving case endings or other words.

The Mahabhasya analogy clarifies this natural hierarchy: Just as one cares for one's own body (internal) before attending to friends (external), grammar rules that rely on the core elements (like the root) take precedence over rules relying on external elements (like suffixes or other words).

docs.title: 3. Relation to Sutra 6.4.22 (असिद्धवदत्राभात्)
docs.text:
The user requested a check on Sutra 6.4.22 Asiddhavad atrabhat (असिद्धवदत्राभात्).

The Sutra:

असिद्धवदत्राभात् (6.4.22) "Asiddhavat atra ā-bhāt"

Meaning: In the section of the Ashtadhyayi beginning with this rule and extending up to the end of the Bha section (technically up to 6.4.129, covering the "Bha" stems), any operation performed is treated as Asiddhavat (as if it has not happened) with respect to any other rule in the same section.

The Connection & Distinction: Both the Paribhasha ("Asiddham bahirangam...") and Sutra 6.4.22 deal with the concept of Asiddhatva (invalidity/suspension of a rule). However, they differ in scope:

  1. Nature:

    • Paribhasha: It is a Nyaya (logical maxim) derived from worldly observation (Loka-nyaya—the person rising in the morning). It applies generally throughout grammar whenever there is a conflict between internal and external operations.

  2. Sutra 6.4.22: It is a Shastra (statutory rule) specifically mandated by Panini. It applies only within the specific section of the text (the Bha prakarana, 6.4.22 to 6.4.129).

  3. Interaction:

    • Sometimes, the Paribhasha is used to justify the order of operations. However, Panini formulated 6.4.22 to handle specific technical conflicts in the Bha section where the general logic might be insufficient or where he wanted to enforce a specific "invisibility" of rules regardless of internal/external status.
    • The Paribhasha essentially says: "Inner wins over Outer."
    • Sutra 6.4.22 says: "Two rules in this specific section are invisible to each other."

Example for 6.4.22 (jahi): In the formation of jahi (Imperative of han, to kill), two rules apply: 1. Substitution of han with ja (6.4.36). 2. Deletion of hi ending (6.4.106). Because of 6.4.22, the substitution ja (which happens first) is considered asiddha (invisible) to the rule trying to delete hi. If ja were visible, the condition for deleting hi (which requires a consonant ending, not a vowel ending like ja) might be violated. The asiddha nature allows the derivation to proceed correctly.

To answer your question directly: You are correct that ktin is generally a seṭ suffix (takes the augment iṭ) when following a causal base. However, in the specific derivation of corti, the augment iṭ is prohibited (making the suffix aniṭ in this context). Once ktin becomes aniṭ, the rule ṇeran iṭi can apply to delete the causal ṇi.

Here is the step-by-step application:

docs.title: 1. The Derivation of Corti (चोर्ति)
docs.text:
Step 1: Formation of the Causal Base * Root: cur (चुर् - to steal, 10th class curādi). * Add Causal Affix: cur + ṇic (nic). * Operation: The root vowel u undergoes guṇa (due to ṇic). * Result: cori (चोरि).

Step 2: Adding the Suffix * Base: cori * Suffix: ktin (ti). * Status: ktin is an ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with a val letter (t), so by default, it should take the augment iṭ (Rule 7.2.35).

Step 3: The Crucial Exception (Blocking iṭ) * For the form corti to exist, the iṭ augment must be blocked. * In specific grammatical interpretations (often involving Varttikas or specific lists like the titutrathasi... rule 7.2.9 applied to specific forms), the iṭ is prohibited for ktin in this context. * Result: The suffix ktin is treated as aniṭ (without iṭ).

Step 4: Application of ṇeran iṭi* * Now we have: cori + ti (where ti is aniṭ). * Rule 6.4.51 ṇeran iṭi: The ṇi (of the causal affix) is elided (deleted) when followed by an aniṭ ārdhadhātuka suffix. * Since we established in Step 3 that ti is aniṭ here, the rule applies. * Operation: cor~i~ + ti → cor + ti*.

Step 5: Final Form * Result: corti (चोर्ति).

docs.title: Addressing Your Confusion
docs.text:
Your question asks: "If ktin isn't aniṭ then how's ṇeran iṭi applied?"

The answer is that ṇeran iṭi is only applied because ktin is treated as aniṭ in this specific case. If ktin were to retain its standard seṭ status (taking iṭ), the derivation would proceed as follows: * cori + i (iṭ) + ti * The suffix is now iti (beginning with a vowel). * ṇeran iṭi cannot apply (requires aniṭ). * Instead, ṇi turns to ay (via ayādeśa). * Result: corayiti (which is the standard, regular form).

Therefore, corti is an exceptional form that exists only because the iṭ augment is blocked, satisfying the condition for ṇeran iṭi to delete the causal marker. 2/9/26, 11:29 PM - मोहित डोकानिया: ॺ 2/9/26, 11:33 PM - +919*0217: Dhanyasmi Mahoday for the detailed explanation. 🙏🙏🙏 2/10/26, 8:21 AM - ~ Markand Joshi left 2/10/26, 7:53 AM - +919*8972: Yes.

docs.title: Why doshavaakyam is incorrect:
docs.text:
1. Grammatical Analysis (Samasa):
    • If analyzed as a Tatpurusha compound (doṣāṇāṁ vākyam), it would mean "a sentence of faults" (a sentence composed entirely of faults), which is semantically odd.
    • If analyzed as a Karmadharaya compound (doṣaḥ eva vākyam), it would mean "the fault is the sentence," implying the sentence itself is a defect, not that it contains one.
    • To mean "a sentence with a fault," you typically need a word like yukta (joined with), sahita (with), or a Bahuvrihi compound structure that modifies the noun. However, doṣavākyam does not follow the standard patterns for this meaning.

docs.title: The Correct Terms:
docs.text:
To express "a sentence with a fault" or "a faulty sentence," you should use one of the following standard terms:

  1. Duṣṭavākyam (दुष्टवाक्यम्) — Most Standard

    • Duṣṭa means "corrupted," "bad," or "defective."
    • This is the standard term used in Sanskrit poetics (Sahitya Shastra) and grammar to refer to a sentence that has a defect (grammatical or semantic).

  2. Sadoṣam Vākyam (सदोषम् वाक्यम्) or Sadoṣavākyam (सदोषवाक्यम्)

    • Sa (with) + doṣa (fault).
    • This literally means "a sentence with a fault" or "a faulty sentence."

  3. Doṣayuktam Vākyam (दोषयुक्तम् वाक्यम्)

    • This explicitly means "a sentence joined/filled with faults."

docs.title: Summary

If you want to say "faulty sentence," use Duṣṭavākyam (दुष्टवाक्यम्). docs.title: 1. एतद् (Etad) - Very, Very Close (समीपतर - Samīpatara)
docs.text:

docs.title: 2. इदम् (Idam) - Near (सन्निकृष्ट - Sannikṛṣṭa)
docs.text:

  • Verdict: Correct.
  • Usage: Used for "This." It indicates proximity but is slightly less immediate than Etad. However, in general usage, Etad and Idam are often used interchangeably for "This."

docs.title: 3. अदस् (Adas) - Remote / Distant (विप्रकृष्ट - Viprakṛṣṭa)
docs.text:
• Your definition: "Far away, in absentia."
  • Verdict: Partially Correct. It denotes "Far away," but usually for objects that are still visible (unlike your "in absentia" guess).
  • Usage: Used for "That over there." Think of pointing at the sun, the moon, or a distant mountain. They are far, but you can see them.
  • Forms: Asau (Masculine/Feminine singular), Adaḥ (Neuter singular).
  • Example: Asau Sūryaḥ (That Sun).

docs.title: 4. तद् (Tad) - Out of Sight / Absent (परोक्ष - Parokṣa)
docs.text:
• Your definition: "So far that our eyes can't see / Parokshe."
  • Verdict: Correct.
  • Usage: Used for "That." Specifically used for things that are absent, out of sight, or referring to something mentioned in the past (anaphoric reference).
  • Example: "Remember that man we met yesterday?" (Use Sah/Tad).

docs.title: Summary of Distance Hierarchy
docs.text:
1. Etad: Closest (Here).
  2. Idam: Close (Here).
  3. Adas: Far (There - Visible).
  4. Tad: Absent (There - Not visible / Mental reference).

docs.title: Are there any other pronouns like this?
docs.text:
Yes, there are a few others you should know:

1. त्यद् (Tyad) - "That" * This is very similar to Tad. In the lists, it often appears as Tyad. * Declension starts: Syaḥ, Tyau, Tye. * It is generally used for well-known things or in poetry, but it functions almost identically to Tad.

2. एनद् (Enad) - The "Substitute" Pronoun * This is a special pronoun used only in the Accusative (2nd), Instrumental (3rd), and Genitive/Locative (6th/7th) dual/plural cases as a replacement for Etad or Idam. * Example: Instead of saying Tam (him), you might see Enam. * Enam = This one/Him (Accusative).

3. यद् (Yad) - The Relative Pronoun * Meaning: "Who/Which." * It is not a distance indicator, but it is essential because it pairs with Tad. * Example: Yad ... Tad (What... That...). "What you sow, that you reap."

4. किम् (Kim) - The Interrogative Pronoun * Meaning: "Who? / What?"

The "Rule Books" (Sources of Authority) The rules for chanting are derived from several ancient texts: * Shiksha (Phonetics): One of the six limbs of the Vedas (Vedangas). It dictates specifically how a mantra must be pronounced. * Grihya Sutras & Dharma Shastras (e.g., Manu Smriti): These texts outline the codes of conduct (Achara), including hygiene (Shaucha) and the appropriate times (Kala) for recitation. * The Agamas: Texts that govern temple rituals and worship, often dictating purity rules.

docs.title: 2. General Rules for Vedic Mantras
docs.text:
According to tradition, for a Vedic mantra to be effective and safe, the following conditions are usually required:

  • Shaucha (Physical Purity): One must have bathed and worn clean clothes. The body is considered the instrument; if the instrument is dirty, the resonance is affected.
  • Desha (Place): The place must be Sattvic (pure). A prayer room, a temple, a riverbank, or a clean spot in nature. One should not chant Vedic mantras in the bathroom, bedroom (while on the bed), or unclean places.
  • Kala (Time): The most effective times are the Sandhyas (junction points): Sunrise, High Noon, and Sunset. Brahma Muhurta (approx. 4:00 AM – 6:00 AM) is considered the best.
  • Asana (Posture): The spine should be straight to allow energy to flow.

docs.title: 3. Suggestions regarding Illness and Menstruation
docs.text: You asked specifically about chanting during illness or "the month" (menstruation). Here is the breakdown based on traditional scripture and modern guidance:

docs.title: A. During Illness (Physical Weakness)
docs.text:
• Loud Chanting (Vaikhari): Discouraged. If you are ill, you may not have the breath control to maintain the correct meter (Chandas) and pitch (Svara). Incorrect chanting of Vedic mantras is said to produce adverse effects. Furthermore, if you haven't bathed due to fever/illness, you lack external purity.
  • The Solution – Listening: It is perfectly acceptable to listen to recordings of the mantras.
  • The Solution – Mental Chanting (Manasika): Most teachers agree that mental chanting has no restrictions. If you repeat the mantra silently in your mind without moving your tongue or lips, rules of physical purity are relaxed, as the mind is believed to be beyond physical dirt.

docs.title: B. During Menstruation (Rajaswala)
docs.text:
• Traditional View: Strictly Prohibited. The Vedas and Dharma Shastras classify this period as Ashaucha (ritual impurity).
    • The Energetic Reason: Vedic chanting generates intense heat (Tapas) and upward-moving energy (Udana/Prana Vayu). Menstruation is a process of cleansing where the body's energy is moving downward (Apana Vayu). Traditionalists argue that chanting powerful Vedic mantras creates an energetic conflict in the body that can harm the woman's health or subtle body.

  • Modern/Liberal View: Some modern spiritual groups (like the Arya Samaj or certain Neo-Vedanta groups) believe God is beyond biology and allow it.

  • The Consensus Advice: Most traditional Gurus suggest pausing Vedic Chanting (like Gayatri or Rudram) during these days.

    • What to do instead? Switch to Nama Japa (Chanting names like "Ram", "Krishna", "Shiva") or simple Slokas/Bhajans. These do not have the strict "sound vibration" rules of the Vedas and act on the level of devotion (Bhakti), which is always permitted.

docs.title: Final Suggestion
docs.text:
If you do not have a Guru who has initiated you into a specific Vedic mantra, the safest and most spiritually potent path during times of illness or impurity is Nama Japa (simply repeating the name of the deity you love) or Manasika Japa (silent mental repetition). docs.title: The Verse
docs.text: मुक्ताफलैः किं मृगपक्षिणां च मृष्टान्नपानं किमु गर्दभानाम्। अन्धस्य दीपो बधिरस्य गीतं मूर्खस्य किं धर्मकथाप्रसङ्गः॥

docs.title: Analysis of किमु
docs.text:
The word किमु is a combination of two elements: 1. किम् (Kim): An interrogative pronoun (neuter, nominative, singular) or an indeclinable (Avyaya) used to ask "what?" or "of what use?". 2. उ (U): An enclitic particle (Nipata) used for emphasis, comparison, or to fill the meter (Pada-purana).

Grammatical Formation: * किम् + उ = किमु * Here, the म् of किम् simply joins with the vowel उ. This is a basic phonetic combination (Sandhi).

docs.title: Functional Explanation
docs.text:
1. Meaning in Context: In this verse, किमु (as well as किं) is used rhetorically. It does not just ask "what," but rather implies "of what use?" or "what is the purpose of?" It highlights the absolute futility of providing something valuable to someone who lacks the capacity to appreciate or use it.

2. Syntactic Role: * किमु acts as an indeclinable (अव्यय) here. * It connects the object (मृष्टान्नपानम् - delicious food and drink) with the recipient (गर्दभानाम् - for donkeys) to question the logic of the relationship.

3. Difference between किं and किमु: While both किं and किमु serve the same rhetorical purpose in this verse, the addition of उ provides: * Emphasis: It intensifies the sense of absurdity. "What use indeed is delicious food to a donkey?" * Metrical Balance: In Sanskrit poetry (Chanda), the extra syllable उ helps maintain the rhythm of the meter.

docs.title: Summary of the Verse Context
docs.text:
The verse lists several useless scenarios: * किं (What use) are pearls to birds/animals? * किमु (What use indeed) is delicious food to donkeys? * What use is a lamp to a blind man or music to a deaf man? * किं (What use) is a religious discourse to a fool?

docs.title: 1. The Correct Usage
docs.text:
Between अनेके शुभाशयाः and अनेकाः शुभाशयाः, the correct form is अनेके शुभाशयाः.

The word शुभाशय is a combination of शुभ (auspicious) and आशय (intent/wish). In Sanskrit, आशय is a masculine (पुल्लिङ्ग) noun. When we use it in the plural to say "wishes," it becomes शुभाशयाः (similar to how रामः becomes रामाः). Since अनेक acts as an adjective for a masculine plural noun, it must take the masculine plural form, which is अनेके.

docs.title: 2. Why "अनेकाः" is Incorrect for Masculine Nouns
docs.text:
You might ask why गज (elephant) becomes गजाः, but अनेक becomes अनेके. This is because Sanskrit classifies words into different categories for declension:

Nouns (संज्ञा): Words like राम, बालक, and गज are standard nouns. Their masculine plural ends in आः. Pronouns (सर्वनाम): Words like सर्व (all), एक (one), and यद् (which) follow the rules of pronouns.

The word अनेक is derived from एक (न + एक = not one). In Sanskrit grammar, एक belongs to the सर्वादि गण (the group of words starting with सर्व), which are treated as pronouns. Therefore, अनेक follows the rules of pronouns, not the rules of standard nouns like गज.

docs.title: 3. The Technical Rule: जसः शी
docs.text:
The transformation of अनेक into अनेके is governed by a specific rule from Panini’s Ashtadhyayi: जसः शी (Sutra 7.1.17).

This rule states that for words categorized as सर्वनाम (pronouns), the nominative plural suffix (जस्) is replaced by ई (शी). * For a standard noun like गज: गज + plural suffix = गजाः. * For a pronoun-like word like अनेक: अनेक + ई results in अनेके (due to गुण सन्धि where 'अ' + 'ई' becomes 'ए').

This is why we say सर्वे (all), एके (some), and अनेके (many), but we say रामाः and गजाः.

docs.title: 4. Analysis of the Sanskrit Lexicon (व्याकरण विश्लेषण)
docs.text:
According to traditional Sanskrit lexicons like the वाचस्पत्यम्, here is a deeper breakdown of the word:

Etymology and Default Number: The word is defined as न एकः (not one). Because it signifies "more than one," it is naturally used in the plural (बहुवचनान्तता) when referring to a count of objects.

Retention of Pronominal Status: Even though अनेक is a compound (नञ्तत्पुरुष समास), it retains its status as a pronoun (सर्वनाम). This is why it undergoes pronoun-specific transformations such as: * Nominative Plural: अनेके (Many) * Genitive Plural: अनेकेषाम् (Of many) — unlike nouns which would end in आनाम्. * Locative: अनेकत्र (In many places).

The Singular Exception: While usually plural, अनेक can be used in the singular when it refers to the "concept" of diversity rather than a count. For example, in the याज्ञवल्क्य स्मृति, it is said: तथात्मैकोऽप्यनेकश्च (The Soul is one and also manifold/diverse). Here, अनेकः is singular because it describes a quality of the Soul. Panini also uses it in the singular in his rule: अनेकमन्यपदार्थे.

docs.title: 5. Gender-Specific Rules
docs.text:
The form of the word "Many" changes depending on the gender of the noun it describes:

Masculine (पुल्लिङ्ग): Use अनेके. Example: अनेके शुभाशयाः (Many good wishes) or अनेके गजाः (Many elephants).

Feminine (स्त्रीलिङ्ग): Use अनेकाः. Example: अनेकाः शुभकामनाः (Many good wishes). Note that for feminine pronouns, the ending happens to look like the noun ending, but the grammatical path is different.

Neuter (नपुंसकलिङ्ग): Use अनेकानि. Example: अनेकानि फलानि (Many fruits).

docs.title: 6. Classical Examples
docs.text: The lexicon cites several famous works to prove these rules: * मनुस्मृति: अनेकानि सहस्राणि (Many thousands) — Neuter plural. * माघ (शिशुपालवध): पतन्त्यनेके जलधेरिवोर्मयः (Many fall like the waves of the ocean) — Masculine plural अनेके. * श्यामास्तोत्र: अनेके सेवन्ते (Many serve you) — Masculine plural अनेके.

docs.title: 1. भव्यभवम् (Bhavyabhavam) as the Vidheya (Predicate)
docs.text: If you treat भव्यभवम् as the Vidheya for the sub-clause, the syntax becomes: "यतः दयाश्रीः भव्यभवम् (यथा तथा) [अस्ति/प्रभवति]" * The Grammar: Since दयाश्रीः is feminine and भव्यभवम् is neuter singular, treating it as a predicate noun creates a gender mismatch. This is a beautiful, expansive way to interpret it!

docs.title: 2. तोय (Toya) = सोम (Soma) and the Lunar Dynasty connection
docs.text: You are absolutely correct about the Medinī Kośa. Classical poets loved using trans-synonymous chains (Paryāyokti or Śleṣa). * If Toya = Jala, and Jala = Soma, then Toya = Soma. * Therefore, तोयदेवम् (Toya-devam) = सोमदेवम् (Soma-devam) = The Lord of the Moon/Lunar Dynasty. * Your connection to Krishna being सोमात्मजात्मज (Descendant of the Moon) perfectly justifies this. In the context of a Viloma-Kāvya—where the poet had virtually no freedom with the syllables—using तोय to secretly mean सोम is a masterstroke of commentary on your part. It is not a semantic stretch; it is excellent Vyākhyāna (exposition).

docs.title: 3. उतासुभूतम् (Utāsubhūtam) and the deeper meaning of आसु (Āsu)
docs.text: Your strongest argument is here. If the author is already hinting at Soma via तोय, then उत (furthermore / moreover) acts as a bridge to deepen that metaphor. * आसु (Āsu): As you pointed out, from the root आङ् + सु (अभिषवे) (to press out), taking the Kvip pratyaya gives us आसु (the act of pressing Soma, or the extracted Soma juice). * आसु-भूतम्: "He who became the Soma juice." * Why is this philosophically profound? docs.title: English Literal Translation & Explanation
docs.text:
Literal Translation: "I bow down to that (Lord Rama), who possesses a noble smile, who is the (cause of) liberation for the daughter of the earth (Sita), and due to whom the very aggregate of the future and the present is the wealth (that is His) compassion; (who, in the form of Krishna) is the scion of the Yadu dynasty, the (cause of) liberation of the giver of death (Putana), the deity of the brilliantly radiant water/soma (Lunar Dynasty), or the one who has become the Soma (or the act of extracting it) Himself."

Explanation (Vyākhyāna): * Single-Sentence Structure (Ekavākyatva): Because the verb Vande (I bow) appears only once in the first line, the entire second line structurally acts in apposition to the first. The poet is stating that Rama and Krishna are the exact same Supreme Entity. The continuous relative clauses flawlessly capture this Vedantic non-duality (Advaita). * Bhavyabhavam (भव्यभवम्): Treated masterfully as a Samāhāra Dvandva compound (the aggregate of the future and the present). It acts as a neuter singular predicate noun. It implies that the Lord's wealth of compassion (Dayāśrīḥ) is not a fleeting emotion, but constitutes the very fabric of all existence—everything happening now and everything yet to come. * Bhavyabhatoyadevam (भव्यभतोयदेवम्): Relying on classical lexicons like the Medinī Kośa (where Toya = Jala = Soma), Toya is interpreted as the Moon (Soma). Thus, He is the beautifully radiant deity of the Lunar Dynasty (Candravamśa). * Utāsubhūtam (उतासुभूतम्): The particle Uta (or) provides another possibility from the previous metaphor. Deriving Āsu from the Vedic root Āṅ + su (to extract Soma juice), it declares that Krishna is not just the Lord of the Lunar line, but has literally become the essence of the Soma juice itself, perfectly echoing Krishna’s own declaration in the Bhagavad Gita (15.13): "I become the juicy Soma..."

This principle is based on an old belief that a crow has only one eyeball, which it can move from its left eye socket to its right one. With this single eye, the crow can see on both sides, making one thing serve two purposes. How it's used in language: Just like the crow's single eye looks in two directions, this rule applies when a single word or phrase in a sentence connects to two different parts of that sentence, even though it's only written once. It's a way of being efficient with words.

The core idea is that a single word in a sentence can apply to two different things, just like a crow's single eye is believed to see in two directions.

Here are the examples from the text explained:

docs.title: Example 1 & 2:
docs.text:
• Sanskrit: विविधैः आसनैः कुम्भैः विचित्रैः करणैरपि। (Vividhaiḥ āsanaiḥ kumbhaiḥ vicitraiḥ karaṇairapi.)
  • Sanskrit (line 2): ‘विचित्रैः’ इति काकाक्षिगोलकन्यायेन उभयत्र संबध्यते। (‘Vicitraiḥ’ iti kākākṣigolakanyāyena ubhayatra saṃbadhyate.)

Explanation:

  • The first line describes different yoga practices: "with various (vividhaiḥ) postures (āsanaiḥ), breath retentions (kumbhaiḥ), and with wonderful (vicitraiḥ) body movements (karaṇairapi)."
  • The key word here is vicitraiḥ (meaning "wonderful" or "varied").
  • The second line explains that the word vicitraiḥ connects to both the breath retentions (kumbhaiḥ) that come before it and the body movements (karaṇairapi) that come after it.
  • So, instead of saying "with wonderful breath retentions and with wonderful body movements," the word "wonderful" (vicitraiḥ) is used just once in the middle to describe both. It acts like the crow's eye, looking forward and backward in the sentence.

docs.title: Example 3 & 4:
docs.text:
• Sanskrit: पदार्थानां स्मारकत्वेऽपि पदमात्रत्वभाजिनः। (Padārthānāṃ smārakatve'pi padamātratvabhājinaḥ.)
  • Sanskrit (line 4): अपि शब्दः काकाक्षिन्यायेन उभयत्रापि संबध्यते। (Api śabdaḥ kākākṣinyāyena ubhayatrāpi saṃbadhyate.)

Explanation:

  • This example focuses on the word api (which can mean "also" or "even").
  • The text explains that the word api is connected to two parts of the phrase by the "Rule of the Crow's Eye" (kākākṣinyāyena).
  • It links to both what comes before it and what comes after it, serving a dual purpose with a single appearance. In this context, it emphasizes both the "reminder" aspect (smārakatve) and the "mere word" aspect (padamātratvabhājinaḥ).

docs.title: Example 5:
docs.text:
• Sanskrit: बलिनाऽद्वर्तमिध्ये वच्यमानं समर्पयेत्। द्वैधीभावेन वर्तेत काकाक्षिवदलाङ्क्षितः। (Balinā'dvartamidhye vacyamānaṃ samarpayet. Dvaidhībhāvena varteta kākākṣivadalāṅkṣitaḥ.)

Explanation:

  • This example uses the simile directly. It advises that when dealing with a powerful person, one should behave with a "two-fold nature" (dvaidhībhāvena).
  • It explicitly says one should act "like the eye of a crow" (kākākṣivat).
  • This means a person should have a dual policy or attitude—appearing to serve one purpose while also being prepared for another. Just as the crow's eye serves both sockets, a person's actions or attention should serve two different functions simultaneously when dealing with a stronger adversary.

docs.title: 2. क्या यह सम्बन्धवाचक है?
docs.text:
हिन्दी और संस्कृत व्याकरण के अनुसार 'नैयायिक' के दो मुख्य संदर्भ हो सकते हैं:

  • सम्बन्धवाचक (Relational): व्यापक अर्थ में, 'नैयायिक' का अर्थ है "न्याय (शास्त्र) से सम्बन्ध रखने वाला"। इस दृष्टि से इसे सम्बन्धवाचक तद्धित प्रत्यय की श्रेणी में रखा जा सकता है, ठीक वैसे ही जैसे 'सामाजिक' (समाज से सम्बन्धित) या 'धार्मिक' (धर्म से सम्बन्धित) शब्द होते हैं।

  • तद्वेत्ति तदधीते (ज्ञाता/अध्ययन करने वाला): संस्कृत व्याकरण के विशेष नियम (पाणिनी सूत्र: तद्वेत्ति तदधीते) के अनुसार, जो किसी शास्त्र को जानता है या उसका अध्ययन करता है, उसे व्यक्त करने के लिए भी इसी प्रत्यय का प्रयोग होता है। चूँकि 'नैयायिक' का अर्थ "न्याय शास्त्र का ज्ञाता" या "तर्कशास्त्री" होता है, इसलिए यह कर्तृवाचक (Agentive) भाव भी देता है (अर्थात् वह व्यक्ति जो न्याय करता है या न्याय शास्त्र जानता है)।

docs.text:
यदि आप विद्यालयी स्तर की हिन्दी व्याकरण की श्रेणियों (जैसे सम्बन्धवाचक, भाववाचक आदि) की बात कर रहे हैं, तो 'नैयायिक' को 'सम्बन्धवाचक तद्धित प्रत्यय' के अंतर्गत ही गिना जाता है, क्योंकि यह 'न्याय' के साथ सम्बन्ध (सम्बन्धित व्यक्ति) को प्रकट कर रहा है।

Instead, when na is attached to a noun, adjective, or indeclinable (like ādṛtya), it forms a Compound Word (Samāsa). Specifically, it is called the Nañ-Tatpurusha Samāsa (नञ्-तत्पुरुष समास).

Here is the distinction:

A. Upasargas (Verbal Prefixes) There is a closed list of 22 specific prefixes in Sanskrit (like pra, parā, apa, sam, anu, av, ā, etc.). These are added directly to verb roots to change the action. * Example: Ā (prefix) + dṛ (root) = Ādṛ (to respect).

B. Nañ (The Negative Particle) Na is a particle (avyaya) that gets compounded with the finished word. * Example: Na + ādṛtya = Anādṛtya. * Grammatically, anādṛtya is not a "root with two prefixes." It is a compound word consisting of two parts: the negator (an) and the gerund (ādṛtya).

docs.title: The Rule of Change
docs.text:
When this negative particle (Nañ) is attached to a word, it changes form based on what follows it:

  1. Before a Consonant: It becomes A (अ).
    • Na + Satya (truth) = Asatya (untruth).
    • Na + Dharma = Adharma.
  2. Before a Vowel: It becomes An (अन्) (to prevent a vowel clash).
    • Na + Ādṛtya = Anādṛtya.
    • Na + Ekam (one) = Anekam (more than one/many).

docs.title: १. सिद्धि प्रक्रिया (Derivation)
docs.text:
'अनादृत्य' शब्द दो चरणों (steps) में बनता है। व्याकरण के 'अन्तरङ्ग' (internal) और 'बहिरङ्ग' (external) नियमों के अनुसार, धातु के समीप वाला उपसर्ग पहले कार्य करता है।

  1. प्रथम चरण (अन्तरङ्ग कार्य): आ + दृ + क्त्वा

    • यहाँ धातु 'दृ' (आदर करना) है और उसके पूर्व 'आ' उपसर्ग लगा है।
    • सूत्र ७.१.३७ कहता है: यदि धातु किसी समास में हो और उसके पूर्व में 'नञ्' (न) न हो, तो 'क्त्वा' के स्थान पर 'ल्यप्' (य) हो जाता है।
    • यहाँ धातु के ठीक पहले 'आ' है, जो कि 'नञ्' नहीं है। अतः सूत्र लागू होता है।
    • आ + दृ + ल्यप् (तुक् का आगम) = आदृत्य (आदर करके)।

  2. द्वितीय चरण (बहिरङ्ग कार्य): न + आदृत्य

    • अब इस 'आदृत्य' शब्द का 'न' (नञ्) के साथ समास (नञ्-तत्पुरुष) होता है।
    • न + आदृत्य = अन् + आदृत्य (नलोपो नञः / तस्मान्नुडचि) = अनादृत्य (आदर न करके)।

docs.title: २. शंका का समाधान: 'अनञ्पूर्वे' नियम यहाँ क्यों नहीं लगा?
docs.text:
सूत्र में 'अनञ्पूर्वे' का अर्थ है कि वह शब्द जो 'क्त्वा' को 'ल्यप्' में बदल रहा है (अर्थात् जो समास का कारण है), वह 'नञ्' नहीं होना चाहिए।

  • अकृत्वा (न + कृत्वा): यहाँ धातु 'कृ' से पूर्व केवल 'न' है। यहाँ समास का पूर्व पद 'नञ्' ही है, इसलिए 'अनञ्पूर्वे' शर्त के कारण 'ल्यप्' नहीं होता। रूप 'अकृत्वा' ही रहता है।
  • अनादृत्य (न + आदृत्य): यहाँ 'ल्यप्' आदेश 'आ' उपसर्ग के कारण हुआ है, न कि 'न' के कारण। चूँकि 'आ' नञ् नहीं है, इसलिए ल्यप् हो गया। बाद में 'न' जुड़ने से वह ल्यप् वापस 'क्त्वा' में नहीं बदलता।

संक्षेप में: 'अनादृत्य' में 'ल्यप्' आदेश 'आ' के कारण हुआ है, जो कि 'अनञ्' (नञ् से भिन्न) है। अतः सूत्र ७.१.३७ यहाँ पूर्णतः लागू होता है और 'अनादृत्य' रूप सिद्ध होता है। 2/26/26, 11:29 PM - +919*4076: Namaste, which section, chapters constitute Upasana Kanda? While the division is sometimes conceptual, specific texts and chapters are historically classified under this section.

docs.title: 1. The Broad Classification: The Aranyakas
docs.text:
In the traditional tripartite division of the Vedas, the Aranyakas (Forest Treatises) constitute the Upasana Kanda. * Karma Kanda: Samhitas & Brahmanas (Rituals & Hymns) * Upasana Kanda: Aranyakas (Meditations & Symbolic Worship) * Jnana Kanda: Upanishads (Pure Knowledge/Metaphysics)

The Aranyakas serve as a bridge. They move the focus from external physical rituals (Yajnas) to internal, mental meditations (Manasika Yajna).

docs.title: 2. Specific Chapters & Sections (The "Vidyas")
docs.text:
Although the Aranyakas are the designated "section," the most vital and well-known Upasanas (meditations) are actually preserved within the early chapters of the major Upanishads. These specific chapters are often studied as part of Upasana Kanda.

Here are the specific chapters and sections that constitute this body of knowledge:

docs.title: A. Chandogya Upanishad (The Treasury of Upasanas)
docs.text: This is the most significant text for Upasana. Its first five chapters are almost entirely dedicated to Vidyas (meditations). * Chapter 1-2: Udgitha Vidya (Meditation on OM as the Prana and the Sun). * Chapter 3: Madhu Vidya (Meditation on the sun as the honey of the gods) and Gayatri Vidya. * Chapter 3 (Section 14): Shandilya Vidya (A famous meditation on the Atman as the "Tajjalan" — that from which the world is born, breathes, and dissolves). * Chapter 4: Samvarga Vidya (Meditation on Air/Prana as the "absorber") and Upakosala Vidya. * Chapter 5: Panchagni Vidya (The Doctrine of Five Fires) and Vaishvanara Vidya (Meditation on the Universal Self).

docs.title: B. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
docs.text: While primarily a text of high metaphysics (Jnana), it opens with profound Upasanas in its early chapters. * Chapter 1, Section 1-2: Ashvamedha Upasana (Meditating on the sacrificial horse as the entire Cosmos—a mental ritual). * Chapter 1, Section 3: Udgitha Brahmana (Meditation on Prana). * Chapter 6, Section 2: Panchagni Vidya (Repeated here with slight variations from Chandogya).

docs.title: C. Taittiriya Upanishad
docs.text: • Chapter 1 (Shiksha Valli): This entire chapter is dedicated to Upasanas, including the Samhita Upasana (meditation on the conjunction of letters/worlds) and the Vyahriti Upasana (meditation on the mystic utterances Bhuh, Bhuvah, Suvah).

docs.title: D. The 32 Brahma Vidyas
docs.text: In the Brahma Sutras (the logical treatise of Vedanta), the Upasana sections are codified into 32 specific Vidyas. These include the ones mentioned above (Shandilya, Madhu, Dahara, etc.). A student of Upasana Kanda studies these specific methodologies of focusing the mind on Brahman with attributes (Saguna Brahman).

docs.title: Summary for Study
docs.text:
If you wish to study the Upasana Kanda, you should look at: 1. The Aranyakas (specifically Aitareya Aranyaka and Taittiriya Aranyaka). 2. Chandogya Upanishad: Chapters 1 through 5. 3. Taittiriya Upanishad: Chapter 1 (Shiksha Valli). 4. docs.title: Word-by-Word Meaning
docs.text:
• हे देवि (He Devi): [Implied] O Goddess!
  • महायोगिसमयी (Mahāyogisamayī): The great Yogi who follows the path of Samayachara (internal worship/meditation).
  • इह (Iha): Here (in this body or practice).
  • नाडीगणजुषः (Nāḍīgaṇajuṣaḥ): Coursing through the multitude (group) of Nadis (energy channels).
  • मरुत (Marutaḥ): The winds (Pranas/Vital breaths).
  • मनोमार्गं (Manomārgaṁ): The path of the mind (mental inclinations/tendencies).
  • जित्वा (Jitvā): Having conquered / controlled.
  • सेन्दुं (Senduṁ): Together with the Moon (Indu refers to the Ida Nadi or left channel).
  • अर्कं (Arkaṁ): The Sun (Arka refers to the Pingala Nadi or right channel).
  • निरुध्य (Nirudhya): Having restrained / blocked (stopping the breath from flowing in Ida and Pingala).
  • शिखया (Śikhayā): By the flame / tip (of the Kundalini fire).
  • दहनम् (Dahanam): The Fire (specifically the latent fire in the Muladhara Chakra).
  • अपि (Api): Also / Even.
  • संज्वाल्य (Saṁjvālya): Having ignited / made to blaze fully.
  • सुषुम्नां (Suṣumnāṁ): The Sushumna Nadi (the central spiritual channel).
  • संयोज्य (Saṁyojya): Having united / connected (the Prana and Fire into the Sushumna).
  • तव (Tava): Your (referring to the Goddess).
  • आज्ञाचक्रस्थं (Ājñācakrasthaṁ): Situated in the Ajna Chakra (the energetic center between the eyebrows).
  • षड्ग्रन्थिशशिनं (Ṣaḍgranthiśaśinaṁ): The Moon associated with the six knots/chakras (Shad = six, Granthi = knots, Shashinam = Moon).
  • श्लथयति (Ślathayati): Loosens / unties (the knots of the chakras).
  • च (Ca): And.
  • विलयति (Vilayati): Melts / Dissolves (causes the nectar/Amrita from the inner Moon to flow).

docs.title: Detailed Explanation:
docs.text:
1. The Pattern: The Gana sequence for all four padas is exactly न न र र र र र र (2 Na-ganas followed by 6 Ra-ganas). This totals 24 syllables per quarter.
  2. Jaati: Because it has exactly 24 syllables per quarter, it belongs to the सङ्कृति (Saṅkṛti) Jaati (class).
  3. Chhanda Name:
  4. In specific metric classifications of Sama-Vrittas (Sanskrit meters with identical quarters), a 24-syllable meter with this exact न न + ६ र pattern is named किरीट (Kirīṭa).
  5. Scholarly Context (Daṇḍaka): The repeating pattern of Na Na followed by a series of Ra ganas is the hallmark signature of the दण्डक (Daṇḍaka) family of meters (such as Caṇḍavṛṣṭiprayāta, which has 27 syllables). Later classical prosodists like Pingala mandated that Dandakas must have more than 26 syllables. However, this specific verse is famously from Bhasa’s Pratimānāṭakam (Act 1, Verse 11). Scholars widely classify this verse as an early, 24-syllable Daṇḍaka, proving Bhasa composed it before the rigid 27-syllable minimum was established.

The General Rule (Compound Word) The word representing Lord Shiva here is पार्वतीपति. This is a compound word (Samasa) made of पार्वती + पति.

According to Sanskrit grammar (Panini Sutra Patiḥ samāsa eva - पतिः समास एव), when पति is at the end of a compound word, it behaves like a regular masculine word ending in 'i' (like हरि or कवि).

  • हरि (Hari) in Chaturthi Vibhakti (Dative Case) becomes हरये.
  • कवि (Kavi) becomes कवये.
  • Therefore, पार्वतीपति behaves exactly like them and becomes पार्वतीपतये.

docs.title: 2. The Exception (Standalone Word)
docs.text:
If you use the word पति all by itself (meaning just "husband" or "master"), it has a special, irregular declension. It does not follow the pattern of हरि.

  • पति (Alone) in Chaturthi Vibhakti becomes पत्ये.

 श्रीकृष्णः - बाधा तु तादृशस्य जनस्य हि सम्भवेत्, यः स्वयं न किमपि जानाति, न वा अन्येषु आदरभावं प्रदर्श्य तेषां वचनं हि मन्यते, सः स्वयं हि संशयात्मा वर्तते, एतादृशः मनुष्यः अवश्यं पतति । तस्य कृते न वा अयं लोकः सुखदः भवेत्, न च परलोकः हि सुखदायी भवितुमर्हेत् । एवम् अज्ञानिनः, संशयात्मनः च मनुष्यस्य न क्वापि सुखदर्शनं सम्भवति ।
अर्जुनः - यदा मनुष्यस्य संशयभावः नश्येत् तदा किं स्यात् ?

अर्जुनः - भगवन् ! ये भोगविषयेषु विरक्ताः स्युः, तेषां किमपि वैशिष्ट्यं स्यात् किम्  ?
 श्रीकृष्णः - आं, महत् वैशिष्ट्यम् अस्ति अर्जुन ! यः मनुष्यः स्वदेहस्य विमोक्षणात् प्राक् कामक्रोधादिभ्यः  समुद्भवं वेगं सोढुं शक्नोति, अर्थात् यदि तत्समये तस्मिन् मनुष्ये कामक्रोधजन्यः वेगः हि उत्पन्नः नैव भवति, तर्हि सः सुखी, योगी, शुरवीरः, सुजनः वा आख्यायते ।
अर्जुनः - तेन वैशिष्ट्येन साधकस्य किं भवेत् भगवन् ?
श्रीकृष्णः - कामक्रोधादिभिः रहितः साधकः परमात्मसम्बद्धं दिव्यसुखम् अनुभवति । सः निर्मलचित्तपुरुषः सर्वदा परमात्मनि एव रमते । तस्य ज्ञानं नित्यं प्रकाशते । सः ब्रह्मस्वरूपः साधकः शान्तं ब्रह्म अधिगच्छति इति तस्य वैशिष्ट्यम् अवगच्छ अर्जुन !
अर्जुनः - अन्ये साधकाः अपि कदाचित् तत् शान्तं, निर्वाणब्रह्म प्राप्नुयुः वा भगवन् ?
श्रीकृष्णः - आम्, अन्ये अपि तत् ब्रह्म प्राप्तुमर्हन्ति अवश्यमपि । येषां शरीरम्, इन्द्रियाणि, मनः च वशीभूतानि सन्ति, येषां मनोगताः सर्वसंशयाः नष्टाः, येषां च समस्तपापानि भस्मीभूतानि सन्ति, ते विवेकवन्तः साधकाः निर्माणब्रह्म प्राप्तुमर्हाः ।
अर्जुनः - एतत् निर्वाणं ब्रह्म प्राप्तवतां पुरुषाणां लक्षणानि कानि स्युः भगवन् ?
श्रीकृष्णः - ते निर्वाणं ब्रह्म प्राप्तवन्तः साधकाः कामक्रोधादिभिः रहिताः भवन्ति । तेषां मनोबुद्ध्यादिकं स्ववशे भवति । ते आत्मस्वरूपस्य साक्षात्कारिणः भवन्ति । एतादृशाः ज्ञानयोगिनः इहलोके, परलोके, सर्वत्र च निर्वाणं ब्रह्म अधिगच्छन्ति ।
अर्जुनः - एतत् निर्वाणं ब्रह्म अन्यविधेन साधनेन अपि प्राप्तुं शक्यं किं केशव ?
 श्रीकृष्णः - आं, शक्यमवश्यम् । ध्यानयोगेन तत् प्राप्तुं शक्यते । यः ध्यानसाधकः बाह्यविषयान् बहिः कृत्वा इत्युक्ते सर्वविषयान् परित्यज्य, स्वकीयां दृष्टिं भ्रुवोर्मध्ये संस्थाप्य च, बाह्याभ्यन्तरे संचारिणौ प्राणापानौ अथवा पूरकरेचकौ समौ करोति, सः इन्द्रियं, मनः, बुद्धिः, इच्छा, भयं, क्रोधः इत्यादिभिः रहितः, मोक्षपरायणः पुरुषः सदा मुक्तः एव स्यात् इति सम्यक् ज्ञायताम् अर्जुन !
अर्जुनः - भगवन् ! इतोऽपि सुगमम् अन्यदपि साधनम् अस्ति किम्, येन मनुष्यः सुखपूर्वकं मुक्तः भवेत् ?
श्रीकृष्णः - इतोऽपि सुगमः तु भक्तियोगः वर्तते । यः मनुष्यः मां सर्वलोकानां महेश्वरं, समस्तप्राणिनां परमं मित्रं, सम्पूर्णयज्ञानां, तपसां च भोक्तारं जानाति, दृढतापूर्वकं मन्यते च, आत्मानं न भोक्तारम्, अपितु केवलं भगवतः दासं मन्यते, सः ब्रह्मरूपां परां शान्तिं लभते इति । (गीता - ५/२०-२९)
 इति श्रीमद्भगवद्गीतामूलग्रन्थम् अनुसृत्य सज्जीकृते सरलप्रश्नोत्तरेऽस्मिन् कर्मसन्यासयोगः नाम पञ्चमोऽध्यायः सम्पूर्णः। श्रीकृष्णार्पणमस्तु ! (अनुवर्तिष्यते)
    -- नारदोपाध्यायः ।

अस्मिन् अध्याये भगवता उक्तं यत् येन केनापि साधनेन अन्तःकरणे समता आनेतव्या भवति इत्येव योगस्य लक्ष्यमपि । अनुकूलप्रतिकूलादिस्थितौ अर्थात् मानापमान-सुखदुःखादिपरिस्थितौ अन्तःकरणे समभावस्य आनयनं विना ध्यानं साधयितुम् अशक्यमेव । मनुष्यः आत्मसंयमी भवेत् इति विषयम् अधिकृत्य भगवता शोकाकुलः अर्जुनः अस्मिन् अध्याये सम्यक् प्रबोधितः प्राप्यते । ततः भगवान् अवदत् एवम् -
 श्रीकृष्णः - अर्जुन ! कर्मयोगस्य विषये इतः पूर्वं बहुधा कथितं मया । एतस्य कर्मयोगस्य मार्मिकता अवश्यं ज्ञातव्या भवता । यः मनुष्यः कर्मफलम् अर्थात् उत्पत्तिविनाशशीलान् पदार्थान् अनाश्रित्य कार्यं करोति, सः हि संन्यासी, योगी वा आख्यायते । यः केवलम् अग्निं त्यजति, अथवा केवलं क्रियां त्यजति, न सः सन्यासी, न च योगी  कथ्यते । अतः पार्थ ! लोके जनाः यं सन्यासम् अथवा सांख्ययोगं कथयन्ति, त्वं तमेव कर्मयोगम् अवगच्छ ।
 अर्जुनः - भगवन् ! योगी अथवा संन्यासी भवितुं चेत् तेन किं कर्तव्यम् ?
 श्रीकृष्णः - तेन मनसि उद्भूतं सङ्कल्पविकल्पादिकं त्यजनीयं भवति । यतोहि स्वमनसि उद्भूतस्य लौकिकविषयजन्यस्य संकल्पविकल्पादिकस्य त्यागं विना न कश्चिदपि योगी भवितुमर्हेत् कदाचिदपि ।
  अर्जुनः - भगवन् ! योगी भवितुं चेत् मुख्यतः किं कारणं स्यात् ?
  श्रीकृष्णः - अर्जुन ! यः योगम् आरोढुम् इच्छति, तादृशस्य साधकस्य कर्तव्यकर्मरूपं कार्यं हि योगारूढे कारणं भवति, एवं तस्य योगारूढस्य शान्तिः एव, अथवा तस्याः शान्तेः अनुपभोगः एव परमात्मनः प्राप्तौ कारणं भवति ।
 अर्जुनः - तस्य योगारूढस्य लक्षणं कीदृशं भवति भगवन् ?
  श्रीकृष्णः - यः इन्द्रियजन्येषु अर्थेषु, कर्मसु च अनासक्तः, एवं यः संकल्परहितः साधकः वर्तते, सः हि योगारूढः कथ्यते, तस्य लक्षणं तादृशमेव भवति अर्जुन !
  अर्जुनः - तर्हि मया किं कर्तव्यं भगवन् ?
 श्रीकृष्णः - मनुष्यमात्रं स्वयम् आत्मानम् उद्धरेत्, आत्मानं न पातयेत् कदाचिदपि । यतोहि सः स्वयमेव स्वस्य मित्रं, शत्रुः च अस्ति । अतः त्वमपि आत्मानम् उद्धर अर्जुन !
अर्जुनः - स्वयमेव कथं वा सः मित्रं, शत्रुः च स्यात् इति स्पष्टं न अवगतं मया, कृपया तत् स्पष्टीकुरु भगवन् ?
 श्रीकृष्णः - तर्हि शृणु, येन स्वयम् आत्मना आत्मा जितः, अर्थात् येन असत्सम्बन्धः त्यक्तः, सः एव स्वयम् आत्मनः मित्रं, सुहृद् वा कथ्यते । परन्तु तद्विपरीततया येन स्वयम् आत्मना आत्मा न जितः, अर्थात् असत्सम्बन्धः न त्यक्तः, सः स्वयमेव स्वस्य शत्रुः आख्यायते । किं ज्ञातं वा अर्जुन ? इति । (गीता - ६/१-६)
     (अनुवर्तिष्यते--)

अर्जुनः - ततः तेन किं करणीयं भगवन् ?

अर्जुनः - केन प्रकारेण तस्मिन् आसने सः ध्यानसाधकः उपविशेत् भगवन् ?
श्रीकृष्णः - देहं, ग्रीवां, शिरः च समम्, अचलं च विधाय, इतस्ततः न अवलोकयन् केवलं स्वनासिकायाः अग्रभागं पश्यन्, सुस्थिरः भूत्वा सः उपविशेत् इति । (गीता -६/७-१३)

 श्रीकृष्णः - हे कुन्तीपुत्र अर्जुन ! योगिकुले लब्धजन्मा सः साधकः पूर्वजन्मार्जितं साधनम् अनायासेन हि प्राप्नोति । तस्मात् सः साधनसिद्ध्यर्थं ततोऽपि तत्परतया प्रयतते ।
 अर्जुनः - योगिनां कुले जन्मना किं स्याद् इति ज्ञातम् । भगवन् ! एतदपि कथय यत् यदि शुचीनां श्रीमतां गृहे तेन साधकेन जन्म लभ्यते, तर्हि ततः तस्य किं स्यात् ?
 श्रीकृष्णः - तादृशे पुण्यकुले लब्धजन्मा, योगभ्रष्टः, भोगपरवशोऽपि, सः पूर्वजन्मकृतेन अभ्यासेन परमात्मनि आकृष्यते ।
 अर्जुनः - भगवन् ! पूर्वाभ्यासस्य सः कीदृशः प्रभावः स्यात्, येन च साधकः सहसा साधने आकृष्यते ?
श्रीकृष्णः - अहो, तात ! योगस्य जिज्ञासुः अपि यदा वेदोक्तानि सकामकर्मफलानि अतिक्रामति, एवं स्थिते सः योगभ्रष्टः साधकः तु साधने आरूढः एव वर्तते नु, तस्य विषये पुनः किं वा वक्तव्यमत्र, अलन्तेन ।
  अर्जुनः - तर्हि भगवन् ! परमात्मनि आकर्षणेन साधकस्य किं भवति ?

अर्जुनः - भगवन् ! तत्पतनं नाम किम् ?
 श्रीकृष्णः - पार्थ ! ये देवपूजकाः स्युः, ते देवान् हि प्राप्नुवन्ति । एवमेव पितृसेवकाः पितृ२न्, भूतप्रेतपूजकाः च  भूतप्रेतान् प्राप्नुवन्ति । परन्तु विशेषः यत् भ्रातः ! मत्पूजकाः भक्ताः प्रत्यक्षतया मामेव अधिगच्छन्ति ।
अर्जुनः - प्रभो ! तव पूजकाः त्वां प्राप्नुवन्ति इति तु सत्यं भाति, परन्तु सा भक्तिरपि अतीव कठिना स्यात् किल, ननु ?
श्रीकृष्णः - नहि अर्जुन ! मत्प्राप्त्यर्थं भक्तैः आचर्यमाणा या भक्तिः, सा तु अत्यन्तं सुगमा वर्तते । यः मद्भक्तः, सः मां प्रीतिपूर्वकं पत्रं पुष्पं फलं जलं च अर्पयति,  मत्परभक्तेन तेन भक्त्या अर्पितं तदुपहारम् अतीव प्रेम्णा स्वयमेव अश्नाम्यहम् ।
अर्जुनः - एवञ्चेत् मया किं कर्तव्यं भगवन् ?
